To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the mechanical deagglomeration of cellulose microfibers in the presence of a polymer leads to a transition from aggregates and gellike structures to single microfibri dispersions.

the application of high-energy mechanical de-agglomeration in presence of CMC leads to transitions from aggregates and gellike structures to dispersions of celluloses microfibrils, which display liquid crystalline ordering.

the application of high energy mechanical deagglomeration to bacterial cellulose microfibri networks in the presence sodium carboxymethy cellulose leads to the formation of dispersions of single fibrils, which are stabilized by the adsorbed CMC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new cellulose-based materials with novel properties.
the phase behavior of cellulose microfiber dispersions in the presence of a polymer additive and the resulting phase transitions.
the development of novel cellulose-based materials with tailored properties.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the high-energy deagglomering in presence of CMC leads to a transition from aggregates and gells to nematic gels and colloidal liquid crystals, respectively, which are all based on single microfibrillar building blocks.
the high energy mechanical deagglomeration in the presence of the CMC leads to the formation of single microfibre dispersions and the formation of a nematic gel-type liquid crystal structure.

the deagglom- eration of BC microfibrils by high-energy mechanical processing leads to a transition from aggregates to a dispersion of single microf fibrils, which is accompanied by a transition from a gel to a liquid crystalline structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

high-energy mechanical de-aggregation in the presence of a suitable surfactant can lead to a significant increase of the ζ potential, and thus to a transition from aggregates and gells to dispersions of individual microfibrils.
high-energy mechanical de-agglomeration in combination with the adsorption of CMC can be used to control the structure of microfibril networks.
we have shown that it is possible to deaggregate cellulose microfibri aggregates by high-energy mechanical processing.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mechanical deagglomeration of cellulose microfibers can be used to tune the phase behavior of cellulose microfiber dispersions and thus to control their rheological properties.
the phase diagram of cellulose dispersions can be manipulated by high-energy mechanical processing and polymer adsorption.
the phase transitions observed in our study are a result of the interplay between mechanical deagglomeration and adsorption of CMC.
